MUNICIPAL EQUIPMENT GUIDE

Dongfeng KT1D Electric Sweeper Truck for Urban Road Cleaning

A specification-first guide to assessing the 4x2 KT1D chassis for street-cleaning work and confirming the sweeper equipment package before purchase.

MODEL GUIDEOctober 8, 20269 min read
In this guideKT1D catalogue dataCleaning route designSweeper equipmentEnergy and chargingOperations and serviceData limitsBuyer checklistFAQ

KT1D catalogue configuration

The project catalogue lists the Dongfeng KT1D as a 4x2 electric sweeper chassis in the 18 t GVW class. The row shows 232 / 266 kWh battery choices, 128 kW rated / 260 kW peak motor output, direct drive, 5,000 mm wheelbase, 6 t / 10 t in the displayed front/rear axle field, 295/80R22.5 tyres, EBS and GB charging. Confirm the exact battery, axle meaning and model code in the supplier's technical sheet; this article does not infer a performance or body specification from those entries.

ItemCatalogue entryWhat to confirm
Drive / weight class4x2 / 18 t GVWCompleted vehicle mass and permitted axle loads
Battery232 / 266 kWhExact pack and approved operating window
Motor / drive128 / 260 kW; direct driveVehicle-specific output and body interfaces
Wheelbase5,000 mmBody mounting and final dimensions
Axle field6 t / 10 tSupplier clarification; not assumed as an approved rating
Tyres / safety / charge295/80R22.5; EBS; GBFinal fitment, equipment and charger match

The 18 t figure is GVW, not payload. Sweeper equipment can add significant mass and the approved payload must be determined for the completed vehicle, with its hopper, water system, suction hardware, auxiliary equipment, occupants and tools. The catalogue row does not name a body supplier or provide an empty-body mass statement.

It also does not specify hopper volume, sweeping width, suction rate, filter class, water capacity, nozzle design or a productivity rate. These are core job requirements and must come from the body builder's technical offer. Do not assume that a chassis model name defines the cleaning performance or that two sweeper bodies can be compared by chassis battery alone.

Translate a municipal cleaning plan into routes

Define what the vehicle is expected to clean: road lanes, curb edges, industrial yards, tunnels, parking areas or another municipal surface. Different debris, dust, lane width and access conditions affect the equipment package and route timing. Document when streets may be closed, how the truck will move through traffic, where it can stop to empty debris, and where water and charging are available. Make separate plans for routine rounds and seasonal or event-related work.

Measure total route distance, elevation, speed, stop frequency, sweeping speed, work time, travel time, dwell and return-to-depot distance. Include deadheading to the first route point, travel between sections, debris unloading and refilling. A short cleaning route may take many hours if it includes slow operation or frequent stops. Conversely, a long travel distance does not describe the hours of powered sweeping. Keep travel and work-mode consumption separate when the equipment supplier can provide measurements.

Check street geometry and restrictions with the completed vehicle dimensions: wheelbase, front and rear overhang, turning path, height, width, ground clearance and axle loads. Inspect parking bays, narrow streets, low structures, ramps, curb transitions and reversing areas. A nominal 4x2 chassis layout does not certify access to any particular road or prove the unit's maneuverability once the body is mounted.

Ask the municipality to prioritize service coverage, required cleaning windows and acceptable revisit frequency. Dispatcher instructions should identify which route segments can be deferred, where equipment must be stopped and how drivers report blocked streets. The route plan must allow safe operations around pedestrians, parked vehicles, road crews and other workers. Local rules and the sweeper manufacturer's instructions remain controlling.

Specify the sweeper body and its interfaces

Prepare a performance brief for the body builder. State target material types, debris size, expected dust, surface, sweeping speed, coverage width, curb-cleaning needs, water use, hopper unloading method and any filtration or noise requirements. Ask the supplier to define the measuring method behind every claimed output. The chassis catalogue cannot answer questions about suction pressure, airflow, hopper capacity or cleaning quality.

Review hopper structure, access doors, dump method, water tank and pump, side brushes, main brush, suction nozzle, filter, hoses and operator controls. Clarify which systems require electrical power, hydraulic power or another drive interface. Confirm continuous and peak loads, duty duration, protection, interlocks, emergency stops and diagnostics. Ask how the system handles a blocked nozzle, full hopper, low water and an equipment fault.

Coordinate the equipment mass and center of gravity with chassis load limits. Request drawings, body mounting details and axle calculations with the hopper empty and in the intended loaded condition. Debris mass is variable, so establish how operators will know when to unload and ensure the completed vehicle remains within its approved mass envelope. Consider the body raised or tilted during unloading as well as the normal travel position.

Preserve access to the charging port, cooling inlets, service panels, cameras, lights and emergency devices. Confirm that sweeping hardware does not obstruct visibility, ground clearance or routine maintenance. The 5,000 mm wheelbase is the catalogue chassis entry; completed overall length and turning geometry require body-specific drawings. Include installation, testing, training and documentation responsibilities in the offer.

Assess the two battery choices realistically

The catalogue lists 232 and 266 kWh options but does not provide validated route range or powered sweeping hours. Energy use will depend on the route, completed mass, travel speed, stop-start pattern, body electrical loads, water and debris mass, temperature and duration of equipment operation. The fact that sweeping is performed slowly does not make the job energy-free; body equipment and auxiliary systems can influence the shift profile.

Use a representative workday to estimate energy. Record starting and return state of charge, distance, travel and sweep hours, water fills, hopper dumps, ambient conditions and charging energy. If no comparable data exists, plan a controlled demonstration or pilot with the selected chassis and body. Define a reserve for detours, extra cleaning sections, equipment operation and charger downtime. Follow the vehicle supplier's approved SOC guidance; do not treat nominal capacity as fully usable routine energy.

Compare whether a 232 or 266 kWh configuration meets the shift with reserve, charging opportunity and the approved vehicle mass. A larger nominal pack may change mass and charge demand; the catalogue does not quantify these trade-offs. Ask for exact pack details and a vehicle-specific energy assessment. Do not quote a fixed distance or hectares per charge without documented test conditions.

Plan charging, wash-down and maintenance

Verify the GB charging inlet on the exact vehicle, connector and communications with the proposed station, site supply and charger output accepted by the truck. Have a qualified professional review electrical capacity, protection, placement, cable reach and load management. Coordinate charging with end-of-shift debris disposal, wash-down, water refill, inspections and the next dispatch. Establish a backup process if the truck returns late or its usual charger is unavailable.

Cleaning equipment can introduce water, grit and debris around components. Follow manufacturer guidance for cleaning, isolation and inspection; do not assume high-pressure wash-down is safe at every location on the vehicle. Agree inspection routines for brushes, suction, filters, hoses, water circuits, hopper seals and body controls as well as tyres, brakes, chassis and high-voltage warnings.

Set support responsibilities between chassis supplier, body builder and municipal workshop. Confirm parts lists, wear components, diagnostics, training and response escalation. A vehicle that cannot sweep because of a small body-side component is still unavailable for its route. Stock appropriate consumables based on the body maker's recommendations and local supply lead times. Keep service records tied to route hours and operating conditions to guide preventive maintenance.

What buyers still need to verify

The catalogue does not establish hopper size, brush dimensions, working width, water volume, cleaning output, range, charge time, price, warranty or complete body package. Its 6 t / 10 t field is displayed beneath front/rear axle, so its precise meaning requires supplier confirmation rather than interpretation. No public-road suitability or approval should be assumed from this generic model line. The image is a special-vehicle family visual, not a claim that it shows a KT1D unit.

Before tender or purchase, request a full vehicle and body specification, mass breakdown, axle calculations, approved interfaces, equipment performance data and destination-market documents. Run an acceptance test on the delivered body and a route trial using representative streets. Define measurable criteria with the municipality rather than relying on general product descriptions.

KT1D buyer checklist

  • Cleaning purpose, debris type, route distance, service window and discharge locations.
  • Exact battery option, model code, motor and completed-vehicle mass.
  • Supplier clarification of the 6 t / 10 t front/rear axle field.
  • Hopper volume, working width, suction/brush package, water and filtration details.
  • Body power requirements, electrical/hydraulic interfaces and emergency controls.
  • Dimensions, turning, axle loads and access on the completed route.
  • Measured energy plan, SOC reserve, charger and site operating schedule.
  • Acceptance criteria, training, maintenance, parts and warranty responsibilities.

Frequently asked questions

What is the listed KT1D battery capacity?

The catalogue lists 232 / 266 kWh options. Confirm which pack and exact model code apply to the ordered vehicle.

What is the KT1D sweeping width?

The available chassis row does not provide working width or cleaning output. Request body-specific data and test conditions from the sweeper supplier.

Is 18 t the amount of debris it can carry?

No. 18 t is the catalogue GVW class. Allowable debris payload depends on completed body mass, axle limits and local approval.

How long can it sweep on one charge?

No validated duration is listed. Measure travel and equipment energy for the actual route and body, keeping an operating reserve.
